subject: mathematics
question_text: Show that sin⁴(π/8) + sin⁴(3π/8) + sin⁴(5π/8) + sin⁴(7π/8) = 3/2.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — name each move in order.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Reduce the four angles to two
steps.margin_note: The idea of the question. 3π/8 and 5π/8 both reduce to cos(π/8), and 7π/8 reduces to sin(π/8) — so the four terms are really two, each appearing twice.

recall.must_convey: That the allied-angle reductions turn the four angles into just sin(π/8) and cos(π/8), each twice.
accept: reduce the angles, three pi by eight and five pi by eight both give cos pi by eight and seven pi by eight gives sin pi by eight
use allied angles so only two distinct values remain
the four terms collapse to two values each appearing twice
allied angles vaadi naalugu angles ni rendu ga marchali
convert them all to pi by eight

steps.why: Nothing can be combined while four different angles are on the page. The reductions are what make the expression a sum of two things, not four.
common_mistakes: Trying to evaluate each fourth power separately.
Getting sin(5π/8) = −cos(π/8) and losing the symmetry.
steps.memory_tip: 3π/8 and 5π/8 both reduce to cos(π/8), and 7π/8 to sin(π/8) — four terms are really two, twice each.

steps.label: Group and use a² + b²
steps.margin_note: First mark. The four terms become 2[sin⁴ + cos⁴], and a⁴ + b⁴ is handled by a² + b² = (a+b)² − 2ab applied to the SQUARES.

recall.must_convey: That the terms group as 2[sin⁴ + cos⁴], and that a² + b² = (a+b)² − 2ab is applied with a = sin² and b = cos², using sin² + cos² = 1.
accept: group into two times sin fourth plus cos fourth then use a squared plus b squared equals a plus b all squared minus two ab
apply the algebraic identity to the squares and use sin squared plus cos squared is one
the bracket becomes one minus two sin squared cos squared
a square plus b square identity vaadi, sin square plus cos square one avthundi
group the four terms into two and apply the identity

steps.why: A fourth power is a square of a square. Treating sin² and cos² as the two quantities is what lets an ordinary algebraic identity do the work.
common_mistakes: Trying to expand the fourth powers directly.
Applying the identity to sin and cos rather than to their squares.
steps.memory_tip: a⁴ + b⁴ is handled by a² + b² = (a+b)² − 2ab applied to the SQUARES.

steps.label: Turn the product into sin(π/4)
steps.margin_note: Last mark. 4sin²cos² is (2 sin cos)², which is sin²(π/4) — and sin(π/4) is 1/√2, so the square is 1/2.

recall.must_convey: That 4sin²cos² is written as [2 sin cos]² = sin²(π/4) = 1/2, giving 2 − 1/2 = 3/2.
accept: four sin squared cos squared is two sin cos all squared which is sin pi by four squared equal to a half
the product becomes sin pi by four squared which is one half
two minus a half is three halves
two sin cos ante sin pi by four, square cheste half vasthundi
the answer is three by two

steps.why: The 4 was arranged so that it could be split as 2 × 2 and absorbed into the double-angle formula. Without it the product would not simplify.
steps.memory_tip: 4sin²cos² is (2 sin cos)² = sin²(π/4), and sin(π/4) = 1/√2, so the square is 1/2.
